description:
I'm the solo founder of OrbitVitals AI, partecipating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Universal Event). I'm looking for 1-2 motivated teammates for November 14-15.

Our goal is to develop an innovative astronaut health-monitoring application combining AI, biomedical science, and data visualization.

Skills in research, data analysis, UX, or software development are welcome. Reliability,collaboration, and ambition to compete at the global leve matter most.
summary:
During long-duration space missions, astronauts need to understand how their health changes over time, rather than simply monitoring individual measurements.
OrbitVitals AI is a research prototype designed to support astronauts and medical teams through personalized physiological monitoring, sleep and activity tracking, nutrition management, cognitive assessments, and explainable artificial intelligence.
The system evaluates data quality, compares measurements against individual historical references, and examines trends to help identify changes that may deserve human attention. A locally operated AI assistant is designed to explain stored results and provide relevant scientific context.
Our interactive demonstration uses clearly labeled synthetic astronaut data. Separately, the project includes reproducible analysis tools for authentic NASA terrestrial analog research datasets.
OrbitVitals AI demonstrates a transparent, human-centered approach to health monitoring for future space exploration. It is not a medical device and does not provide diagnoses or treatment recommendations.
details:
The Problem

During long-duration space missions, astronauts encounter physiological and operational challenges associated with altered gravity, disrupted sleep, isolation, demanding schedules, and constrained access to medical support.

Individual measurements do not always reveal whether a value is unusual for a particular astronaut. Differences between personal baselines, changing conditions, missing observations, and uncertain data quality can complicate interpretation.

A monitoring system should therefore do more than display numerical readings. It should distinguish measurement reliability from physiological interpretation, evaluate changes over time, and communicate uncertainty clearly.

Our Solution

OrbitVitals AI is an astronaut health-monitoring research prototype that combines an interactive web platform, personalized physiological references, longitudinal analysis, and explainable artificial intelligence.

The application provides two complementary perspectives.

Crew Interface: An astronaut-centered workspace for reviewing physiological indicators, personal trends, sleep, physical activity, nutrition, hydration, daily check-ins, and cognitive assessments.

Medical Interface: A separate overview for reviewing the crew's information, examining individual trends, identifying flagged observations, and supporting human oversight.

The system is designed around three essential questions:

  1. Is the available measurement reliable enough to interpret?
  2. How does it compare with the astronaut's own historical reference?
  3. Does the available history suggest a change worth reviewing?

When the evidence is insufficient, OrbitVitals AI preserves uncertainty rather than inventing a conclusion.

Technical Implementation

The platform uses a React and TypeScript frontend connected to a Python FastAPI backend.

The frontend provides interactive dashboards, historical mission-day navigation, physiological charts, nutrition tracking, exercise information, sleep planning, and crew-specific views.

The backend manages structured observations and implements separate scientific processing components for data quality, personal baselines, and longitudinal evaluation.

These components distinguish missing or questionable measurements from meaningful changes in otherwise usable observations.

The AI architecture uses a locally operated language-model service, scientific evidence retrieval, and safeguards designed to ground explanations in information supplied by the backend.

An optional biomedical review component uses Google's MedGemma model where supported and configured.

The assistant is intended to provide understandable explanations, preserve scientific uncertainty, and support human review. It does not replace the underlying scientific algorithms or independently determine diagnoses.

The system also includes a cognitive assessment module and reproducible tools for investigating selected NASA research datasets.

NASA Resources and Scientific Methodology

NASA research provides the scientific context for the project, particularly the Human Research Program's work on the risks of human spaceflight, sleep disruption, physical activity, and physiological adaptation.

The project also includes separate processing pipelines for two authentic datasets from NASA's Life Sciences Data Archive:

UTMB Bedrest Campaign 1 Actigraphy: A terrestrial analog study containing processed sleep-related observations, including sleep duration and efficiency.

UTMB Bedrest Campaign 3 MR001G Tilt: A terrestrial analog study containing cardiovascular observations from tilt testing.

These datasets originate from studies involving human volunteers on Earth, not astronauts in space.

The dataset-analysis pipelines preserve source provenance, missing values, processing limitations, and unresolved metadata where applicable.

Importantly, the interactive astronaut dashboard uses synthetic, simulated measurements. The authentic NASA observations are not presented as the measurements of the simulated crew.

The scientific methods emphasize individual comparison, data-quality assessment, descriptive statistics, longitudinal trends, and traceable explanations.

Innovation and Intended Impact

OrbitVitals AI combines several complementary capabilities within a single astronaut-centered workflow:

  • Personalized interpretation instead of relying exclusively on population-wide thresholds.
  • Explicit separation of measurement quality and physiological evaluation.
  • Historical trends that preserve missing observations and uncertainty.
  • A coordinated Crew and Medical interface.
  • Explainable AI grounded in structured records and scientific references.
  • Local AI operation as a potential foundation for environments with limited connectivity.

The main innovation is the integration of these capabilities into an understandable research prototype, rather than the invention of a new medical algorithm.

The intended long-term impact is to support situational awareness, clearer communication, and informed human review during increasingly autonomous space missions.

Limitations and Responsible AI

OrbitVitals AI is a research and educational prototype, not a certified medical device or flight-qualified health-monitoring system.

All astronaut measurements shown in the interactive demonstration are synthetic or simulated.

The use of NASA research materials does not imply NASA endorsement, clinical validation, or proof that the system performs reliably in spaceflight.

The project does not establish diagnostic accuracy, medical effectiveness, or validated clinical thresholds.

AI-generated explanations must remain subject to verification and human oversight. The system is not intended to prescribe medication, diagnose conditions, or replace professional medical judgment.

Future development would require validated sensor inputs, expert-defined operational requirements, privacy and security assessments, human-factors testing, and independent evaluation using appropriately authorized real-world data.

Our goal is to demonstrate how transparent scientific processing, personalized monitoring, and responsible AI can work together to support future space exploration.
